This brief word-by-word commentary on the *Tadabhyudaya-tantra* is being written preceded by an homage to Śrī Heruka.
1. "Now," and so forth.

The "Secret" refers to the Blessed One, Śrī Heruka; this is stated as the subject matter (*abhidheya*). "Having known and having meditated upon" refers to the path (*mārga*). The practitioner, the yogin, attains—that is, reaches—the siddhi of Mahāmudrā by means of that very Blessed One, through non-differentiation from himself; this is stated as the purpose (*prayojana*). Thus, the Blessed One himself is stated to be both the path and the fruit. The distinction, however, is made on the basis of being with stains (*samala*) or without stains (*amala*). % 1.2

"Not," and so forth. The word "of one who is free from conceptual constructions such as lunar days (*tithi*) and so on" should be understood as ending in the genitive case. Alternatively, it may be construed as "of him for whom there is no lunar day," and so on. "Time" (*velā*) refers to the time of the twilights (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth.

For the yogin who practices the worldly (*grāmya*) dharma characterized by meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), which arises from the village of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), accomplishment (*siddhi*) of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) occurs in the Kali Age during the fourth moment of the drop (*bindu*), which is characterized by the non-perception of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

In the Kṛta Yuga, during the moment of cessation (*virama-kṣaṇa*), there is the accomplishment of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*). It is "single-fold" by means of the mere knowledge of wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*) which is without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), or by means of the mere knowledge of method (*upāya-jñāna*) which is with appearance (*sābhāsa*). In the Tretā Yuga, during the moments of looking, speaking, embracing, and the arising of bliss, there is the accomplishment of bliss; it is "twice-fold" by means of the mere knowledge of both wisdom and method.

In the *dvāpara* age, at the supreme moment (*paramakṣaṇa*), accomplishment (*siddhi*) is sixfold; that is, in the supreme moment—the final moment of the union of the vajra and lotus, characterized by both striking and non-striking—there is the accomplishment of the Supreme. It is threefold through the mere knowledge of female, male, and neuter. In the *kali* age, accomplishment consists of the four moments: the moment of the single flavor of the drops (*bindu*), [the moment of] the four drops becoming a single flavor, and the four qualities which are of a single form. In the *kali* age, during the dwelling in the womb, the first is the embryo (*kalala*) and the limbs such as hands and feet; the second is the sense organs and so forth.

The arising of consciousness is the third; the departure is the fourth—thus there are four. These are the four wheels, the four moments, and the four mudrās; this is spontaneously accomplished, of this there is no doubt. With respect to one, ten, one hundred, and one thousand [lifetimes], the terms beginning with "one-fold" and so forth are to be applied accordingly. In the Kṛta Yuga, it is "one moment," which by reverse order means [attainment] after one thousand births. In the Tretā Yuga, it is "two-fold," meaning after ten births. In the Dvāpara Yuga, it is "three-fold," meaning after one hundred births. In the Kali Yuga, it is "four-fold," which by reverse order means attainment in a single birth.
The chapter that explains the procedure for entering the attainments according to the stated sequence is thus concluded; this is the commentary on the first chapter of the *Śrīherukābhyudaya*.
Then, etc.

Having performed the protection for Śrī Heruka’s great mantra by means of the vowels and consonants, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) through the form of the deity, the armor-mantras (*kavaca*), the vajra-cage (*vajrapañjara*), the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), and so forth.

2.4 The wise one is one who knows the extraction of mantras, who is perfectly pure, and who observes the commitments (*samaya*). "All" [means] because all things pervade the *dharmadhātu* by way of having the form of the seal (*mudrā*) of the *dharmadhātu*. The woman-seal (*strīmudrā*) has the form of the letter *e*. "With a pericarp" means a lotus with eight petals and a central pericarp. On the eight petals, the eight groups of consonants (*varga*) are to be written.

Therein, on the eastern petal is the group of vowels (*svaravarga*). It begins with the *visarga*, that is, the *visarjanīya* sound *aḥ*; that which has this as its beginning is so described. Following that is the vowel *āṃ* together with the *anusvāra*. Following that is the long vowel beginning with *au*. Following that is the short vowel beginning with *o*. In the order of writing—*aḥ, aṃ, au, o, ai, e, ḹ, ḷ, ṝ, ṛ, ū, u, ī, i, ā, a*—there are four categories of vowels distinguished by *visarga*, *anusvāra*, long, and short.
In the two triangles, the extraction of seven syllables will be explained.

He states another terminology for the vowels (*svarasaṃjñā*): "The *saṃyukta* (conjoined) is the pair; the *anusvāra* and *visarjanīya*, as well as the syllables *aṃ* and *aḥ*, are neuter because they consist of one or two dots joined with the vowel *a*; the long vowel is female; the short vowel is male. Thus there are four names. [Note:
*aṃkārāḥkārāv akārayor* is an editorial emendation; the manuscript and edition read *aṅkārāḥkāravakārayor*.]
The second vowel of the group of vowels beginning with *o* is short;

the second [vowel] of the first [group], beginning with *au*, is long. This is the explanation of the designations "female" (*strī*) and "male" (*puṃs*), as well as the explanation of the designations "short" (*hrasva*) and "long" (*dīrgha*).

In the lotus of the *puṇḍra* yantra, one should place the group of vowels in reverse order upon the seven petals starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and south (Yāmya), and the seven consonant groups beginning with the second (*ca*) in forward order. The guttural group (*ka-varga*) is the *jihvāmūlīya*; the palatal group (*ca-varga*) is the *visarjanīya*; and the retroflex group (*ṭa-varga*) is the *upadhmānīya*.

2.8 The *tavarga* (dental class), the *pavarga* (labial class), the *antasthavarga* (semivowel class), and the *ūṣmavarga* (sibilant class). The dissolution (*saṃhāra*) and abandonment of the final letter *kṣa*: having abandoned the letter *kṣa*, the letter *ha* is desired in the *varaṭaka*. The dissolution and non-existence of the final *ūṣman*, the letter *ha*, occurs upon the petals. Alternatively, it exists in the grid (*prastāra*) by implication; thus, [the word] "together" (*saha*) is intended for the *varaṭaka* according to the Teacher’s intention. || 2 ||
*Athetyādi* | The extraction of the eight words.

The eight-syllable mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ* is of the nature of skillful means (*upāya*) and accomplishes ritual actions (*karmasādhaka*). That which begins with *kara kara* and so forth is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). When combined in their entirety, the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) performs all activities.
3.22 All mantras should be known as beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the syllable *phaṭ*.
"Then," and so forth; this is the extraction of the four mantras.

The heart is the essence; it is the four-faced mantra because it is the most excellent of all victorious mantras. It is "the victory over the three worlds" because [it brings about] victory over the three worlds.
Regarding the extraction of the four-faced mantra:
the phrase "beginning with the syllable *oṃ*" is understood to carry over.
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ |
"Ānaya ho bhagavān vajra hūṃ phaṭ!
This mantra has four faces because it possesses four faces and because it accomplishes the four activities, such as pacification and the rest. (4)
Now, beginning with "atha" and so forth...

Now, the application of vowels to the eight syllables of the Blessed One’s name: *namo bhagavate vīrāṇāṃ vīreṣu*. In the syllables of Kālī, there are the Yoginīs and the Ālis; of Mātra, there are the Mātrās.

Union is considered beneficial when understood. For those yogins who have realized the non-duality of the Lord’s self, who know the rules for the recitation of mantras, and who know the abiding of the four wheels and so forth, there is accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Dharma is the *dharmakāya*; desire is the *saṃbhogakāya*.

*Artha* means that which is sought; it is liberation, the deliverance from miserable rebirths and so forth. That [body] by virtue of which this is obtained is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Its mantra is as follows: || 5 ||
Then, etc. (athetyādi).

The *upahṛdaya* (subsidiary heart-mantra) is said to be established through recitation with respect to the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra). It was hidden elsewhere, but here, in this great ocean of oral tradition, it continues: "I, who am knowledgeable in the ritual application of mantras, shall explain it.

With the words beginning with "the fiftieth" (*pañcāśa*), the extraction of the seven syllables is shown: the fiftieth with respect to the eight groups of consonants is the letter *kṣa*; above that is the preceding letter, *ha*.
The letter *ha* [is indicated by the manuscript;

the edition reads *u*]. The meaning is "above the fifty. Of the *mātrikā*, that is, of the group of vowels. "Two" is an indication using repetition (*vīpsā*), meaning two and two. Of the two measures (*mātrā*), the second measure—of that [second measure] as well, the second measure is the vowel *ī*. The meaning is "the fourth. 6.3

The abode of all accomplishments is the two *bindus*. Vajrasattva, who delights the heart of the Yoginīs, is the syllable *repha* (*ra*). Encircled by those two is *hrīḥ*. The ninth letter, *ha*, resides in the position of the ninth pericarp. The thirty-third letter is also *ha*. There are two *ha*s in the pair of letters. "Each one" means they are individually distinct yet joined in reverse order with the two twelfth *mātrās*, the two *ha*s. And those two are honored as the fifteenth: *huṃ huṃ*.

The great ḍākinī Vairocanī is the syllable *oṃ*. "By Māra" means killing, which is the syllable *phaṭ*. She is surrounded and encased by these two. There is a reading in some places as *mārgeṇa*; even there, through the elision of the letter *ga*, it remains *māraṇa*, and thus the meaning is the same. *Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha huṃ huṃ phaṭ*. (Note:
This provides an alternative explanation for the preceding.)

Now, the fiftieth is the letter *kṣa*; that itself is the ninth because it stands outside the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*). Beyond that, what is it? It is the thirty-third, *ha*. That indeed is the "Delight of the Heart" (*hṛdayanandana*). Encircled by the twelve vowels—specifically by the two pairs of second-long vowels (i.e., *ī*, *ū*, *ai*, *au*)—it is honored with fifteen [syllables]. The meaning is: *hāṃ hāṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ*.

[Regarding] the second long [vowels], on the path of the Great Ḍākinī (*mahāḍākinīmārga*), it is surrounded by *oṃ* and *phaṭ*: *oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ phaṭ*. And right here, there is an extraction (*uddhāra*) containing the short vowels.
Is it *sic*? Or is it a case of double sandhi?
By that very [method], it is obtained when joined as *ha hi hu he ho ha*.
[labhyate: ms., lambate ed.]

And regarding this extraction, according to the statement "hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ—thus, each letter is divided by two," there are three *ha* letters: the fifty-first *ha*, the ninth *ha*, and the thirty-third *ha*. These are encircled by the two [groups] of the Mātṛkā. The second vowel is *ā* in the forward order (*anuloma*). Joined with that is the first *hā*. Indeed, the class of vowels is divided fourfold: the short class, the long class, the neuter class, and the conjunct class. Therein, with respect to the long class, the second vowel is *ī*. With that, the second is *hī*.

In reverse order, with respect to the short vowels, the second *mātrā* is *e*. With that, the second [syllable] is *he*. These two syllables, *hī* and *hekāra*, one should cause to be pierced—that is, split—by the letter *ra*, which is the "delight of the Yoginī’s heart" (*yoginīhṛdayanandana*) and [the essence of] Vajrasattva. Thus, it becomes *hrī hre*. Then, the fourth is *ha*, the abode of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhālaya*). "By twelve *mātrās*" means by the twelfth *mātrā*, which is the vowel *u*.

"Thus" (*tathā*) is distinct. One should make each [syllable] individually worshipped fifteen times, with the half-moon and bindu upon its head. Then: *hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ huṃ*. *Mahāḍākinī Vairocanī oṃ. Māraṇaṃ phaṭ*. Encircled on all sides by those two and centered within them, then: *oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ huṃ phaṭ*—this is the extraction of the syllables of the armor of the Six Heroines (*Ṣaḍvīriṇī*). % 6.5-6

The female messengers (dūtīs) established through the *anuloma* and other [practices] abide in the union (*melaka*) of the external and internal. The yoga of Heruka is the sixth moment (*kṣaṇa*). The mudrā is Vārāhī and the seventh moment. Soma is honey and semen; *caru* is the unstruck (*anāhata*).
There is a single meal, as well as the senses and so forth. There is nothing superior to this. 6.
"Then," and so forth.
Fat and oil; some say "flesh" [refers to] menstrual blood and dust.
Semen is "arisen from nectar" (*amṛtodbhava*).
Curd is the brain; some say it is feces.
*Maṣṭikaṃ* (is the reading).
Milk is the water of the thunderbolt.
The Gaṇamaṇḍala is the foremost of all maṇḍalas.
One should take the ritual substance (samayadravya) drawn from the *dharmodayā* and prepared through union, consecrated with the mantra beginning with "Oṃ sarva... and so forth.
"Vajra," and so forth.
The skull-cup is the lotus.
Having prepared the substance with the joined palms of the skull-cup through the union of the vajra and the lotus, the worship should be performed.
Having taken up the *mudrā* with the *kamalāvarta*, one should perform worship.
One should understand this worship to be the worship of the Buddha. Thus, through the stages of the arisen (*utpanna*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), there is accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Mahāmudrā is great wisdom and is of inconceivable form.
"Therein" refers to the region of the yogi and to the worship of the mudrā.
It also refers to the Great Yoga, the yoga of the vow (saṃvara), and the mudrā.
The Buddha-cūḍāmaṇi is sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata;
Vārāhī has her own seal;
the weapon is a curved knife (kartṛ).
The skull-cup is a lotus;
the single seat is the essence of all phenomena;
earth is the form of earth.
The semen is space and that bliss is likewise;
she stands embraced—Vārāhī embraced by the hand of Heruka. "In this way" means by way of both external and internal form.
"Earth," and so forth, refers to the earth-seal (*pṛthivīmudrā*).
The meaning is that one should perform the ritual action after having performed the application of the seal (*mudrāyoga*). || 7 ||
"Then," and so forth.
The Yoginī Vārāhī is joined with the seal (mudrā) non-dual with the Hero; from that, the commencement of all rites [occurs]. || 8 ||
% 9 "Tata" and so forth.
The sequence for both the garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*) is similar, beginning with "Śrī" and so forth, as well as the union of the two (*ubhayasamāpatti*).

This is because of the mention of "one hundred thousand" (*lakṣa*) and "not one hundred thousand" (*alakṣa*), and because of the extensive mention of three hundred thousand. "From the hundred thousand" refers to the moment of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). The "three hundred thousand" refers to the three blisses (*ānanda*) of the generation stage (*utpatti*), the completion stage (*utpanna*), and the ultimate perfection (*pariniṣpanna*).
9.3 One who has not recited [the mantra] and has not performed prior service;
"By all," and so forth, refers to the perfected stage (*pariniṣpannakrama*).
Recollection of the perfected stage is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Knowledge is the sequence of the four wheels;
it is that very same pervasive nature of the *dharmadhātu*, whose form is equal bliss, and which pervades all activities because it performs them.
One should recite and meditate upon the inconceivable; for one who is engaged in all worldly activities, the accomplishments (*siddhis*) are spontaneously attained.
[The word] *svayam eva* is found in the manuscript after correction (*ms. pc.*), while *svarūpam eva* is found in the manuscript before correction (*ms. ac.*) and in the edition.
From the letters, which are the objects such as form and so forth, the object is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is the "eating. || 9 ||
Then, etc. (tata ityādi).
One should recite the mantra after having offered incense to the Blessed Lady depicted on the cloth within the maṇḍala of the deities, with a desire for one’s own intended action.
(Note: The Tantra appears to state that the incense is made from cat excrement.

Then, having entered into union with his own mudrā in the form of Vārāhī, he should perform the oblation; indeed, the entire oblation is performed after drinking the soma. Having drunk it, he remembers and offers the vomited ghee as an oblation. || 10 ||
11. "Then," and so forth. [The editor's emendation changes *cāstaghṛtam* to *cāṣṭaghṛtam*.]

By the Hero, the Blessed One, and by the Heroine, there is the secret worship consisting of consumption and so forth, which is the constant embrace of the non-dual and indivisible [state] for those yogins who possess the perpetual upward-pointing *liṅga*. This is because of that state of being an upward-pointing *liṅga*. The *piśāca* is the *śākhoṭaka* tree or the *abhayā* plant.
Bhūmilabhā is kiñculaka;
pāṭhā is aviddhakarṇī;
rajanī is black turmeric (kṛṣṇaharidrā).
And another [method] is well known:
in this manner, one prepares a single *prastha* of elixir (*rasāyana*); one should smear the penis with the powder mixed with one's own semen, as well as one's beloved woman.
*Striyam* (a woman) according to the manuscript; *śriyam* (prosperity) according to the edition.
*Tadgṛham* means his own house or another's house. *Avikā* means a ewe; *gaḍḍarikā* refers to a chain of blind imitation.
Its dust and blood become the male sheep;
[it is] the wool of the sheep.

One should touch a woman or a man with *svayaṃbhūkusuma* (red lotus), one’s own blood, or one’s own semen. By means of that substance, the penis becomes as expansive as a lotus; some say it also results in the non-erection of the penis.
"Seven," and so forth: wherever one goes, all desired women come there. (11)
% 12 Now, etc.
The practitioner, with the yoginīs residing in his limbs, should be depicted on the cloth of accomplishment (siddhipaṭa), as well as the painter.
The mudrā should be worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
Having entered meditative absorption, facing westward, he should paint and accomplish the cloth-painting (paṭa) facing eastward.
One should bring oneself to perfection in that form.
Through union with Vārāhī’s own mudrā, and through worship of Heruka-Vārāhī, the siddhi of Mahāmudrā is attained.

This mudrā—which is a form pervading the three worlds—is accomplished as characterized by the direct realization of the total abandonment of all afflictions and cognitive obscurations, along with their residual habitual tendencies.
The editor prints: "She is known as the one who directly removes obstructions, the illustrious one. || 12 ||
Now, "atha" and so forth.
By consuming that, O Bhāva, there shall be accomplishment;
the accomplished one, the bestower of accomplishment, the Hero Heruka, remains with his body present, facing all directions, with four faces and so forth.
"From everywhere" means that which has the form of the seven mothers, the seven births, and Vārāhī; it is the nature of mind, non-mind, and consciousness, empty of apprehension.
[The phrase] "with hands," etc., is because of its pervasiveness as the *dharmadhātu*.

"From one's own [body]," and so forth. Having emanated ḍākinīs from one's own body, one causes them to enter the victim through the anus; then, having extracted the seed—the life-force (*jīva*)—and the seed such as semen and so forth from the victim, the sacrificial animal, by way of the channels of the nine apertures, one should cause it to enter one's own body. "In fire," and so forth. Then, having drawn [the victim] out and heated him in a fire kindled by fierce winds, one should visualize him being devoured by the ḍākinīs.
"Bound," and so forth: by means of meditation, the *ḍākinīs* are dispatched to effect that attraction. "Subdued," and so forth: that is the subjugation [of them];
they follow of their own accord.
Ahalyā means that which is immovable and irreversible.
Saṃpradāya is the instruction of the guru.
This alone is said to be the cause of welfare and happiness. || 13 ||
Now, "atha" and so forth.
The collective meaning is that this mandala consists of five layers and comprises sixty-five [deities].
The four-petaled lotus is the "four-lotus.
What is that? It is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). In the center of that great wheel is the Hero, non-dual with the Yoginīs.
*Caturthyādi* etc. "Four lotuses" means four groups of lotuses (*catuṣpadmāni*).
[3v] Four groups of lotuses.
One lotus is described; outside of that is an eight-petaled one; outside of that, a sixteen-petaled one; and outside of that, a thirty-two-petaled one. That is the central Samaya-maṇḍala.

On the four petals are the four [deities] beginning with Ḍākinī. On the eight and sixteen petals are the twenty-four beginning with Pracaṇḍā. On the thirty-two petals are the thirty-two beginning with Yāminī. At the gates are the four: Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrasphoṭī, and Vajrāveśī.
Having first performed that [initial] worship, he then performed another worship with that semen.
Straight means not crooked;
"not crooked" [in this context] refers to being elevated and tapering.
Wrinkled means not spread out.
"Deficient" refers to being either too thick or too thin;
"neither deficiently thick nor thin" is the reading of the editor.
Below the navel it is deficient;
above [the navel] it is excessive.
Then, and so forth: four, twenty-four, thirty-two, and four, making sixty-four;
Rukmiṇī and Satyavāmā are the two Yogeśvarīs who are virtuous (satī).
[Note: *yogeśvaryau* is corrected by the editor; the manuscript reads *yogeśvayau*.]
"Avāmā" refers to the Vidyā Vārāhī of one's own Bhagavat.
"Siddhāḥ" means well-known;
[they were established] previously in the eastern maṇḍala.
These twenty-eight [deities], beginning with Khaṇḍarohā, belong to the *garbha* (womb/interior), that is, they are connected to the *garbha*;

the meaning is that they reside within the four, eight, and sixteen-petalled [lotuses] of the *garbha*. Because that is the *garbha* of the thirty-two-petalled lotus, by implication, Yāminī and the others are located outside the *garbha*.
And by virtue of their functional capacity alone, there are female gatekeepers at the gates.
The mantras for all of them are: Oṃkāra, Nāma, Huṃ, Huṃ, Phaṭ. These are to be worshipped and meditated upon; they are those [mantras].
All [are] all.
The sister and so forth, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and the worship;

"therein" means in the lotus-vessel of the maṇḍala. Having brought the disciple—who has been purified with cat-feces and so forth and whose face is bound with a cloth—facing south, the preceptor, having protected him with the *Gāyatrī* beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, should cause him to enter by means of the ritual of the questions and answers regarding *Potāṅgī* and *Pratipotāṅgī*, and place him within that [vessel].

Having consecrated it with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should recite:
"May Vīraheruka impel that [mantra] of mine belonging to Vārāhī. One should then perform the recitation.
It foretells death for one afflicted by recitation in dreams and the like.
Having recited and made supplication, one should sleep while [contemplating] the life-force of oneself and others as "I" and "mine."
"By one" means by the *gāyatrī*.

Having worshipped a painting or similar object in a solitary place for three nights, one should recite the *gāyatrī* from dawn until the end of the third day and night through union with one's own mudrā. Thereafter, one will possess a divine body and so forth. || 14 ||
"Then," and so forth.

For the sake of establishing one's own self or for the sake of favoring worthy disciples, one should perform the *gaṇamaṇḍala* on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and other such occasions, together with sixteen yogins who possess wisdom.

Then, having recited the Vārāhī mantra and performed protection with the Sumbha and other mantras, one should form a circle (*maṇḍala*), worship the messenger (*dūtī*), and perform the gathering of disciples and so forth.
There are sixteen heroes residing with two messengers.
One should perform every rite through the yogas, that is, the yogas of the deities. Listen, for this has been declared by me only for those who have obtained the knowledge of initiation. 15.8
The medium and superior breathings, the five lamps,
scented water, and the five nectars; having consumed the pill, there is meditative cultivation.
15.9 One should worship the *dūtī* at the beginning of the *gaṇamaṇḍala* and other such rites.
The lowest are those born of mantra;
the highest are the innate (sahaja);
the middling are those born of the field (kṣetraja).
Through these, success shall belong to that yogin.

Regarding the verse beginning with "Śrī" and so forth: one should worship, according to the prescribed rite, the assembly of yogins and yoginīs—who arise from the mantra and mudrā of the Heruka yoga—with foods, drinks, and other offerings.
15.11 One should meditate on a single flower, first as dust, being processed by the vajra and lotus, situated within a skull-cup, and to be consumed.
[ekapuṣpa ms., ekam asya ed.]
With his hand, he should perform the consumption of that *devatācakra*; thus, using two vessels, he should prepare the *caru* offering entirely consecrated [with mantras].
She who is wise in mantra and tantra is a knower of reality (*tattvajñā*).
Of whichever caste, such as the twice-born (dvija) and so forth;
"the pedestal for the Garuḍa on the face" means the grasping of the *bodhicitta* situated upon the lotus of wisdom by means of the mouth.
"Five" refers to the five sense-faculties (*indriya*). "The slaughter of cows" refers to these [faculties]. Combined with these, it becomes "noble" (*udārā*), meaning great.
Situated there, resting upon the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*), and resting within the skull-cup of *caru*;
[this is] the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), the heating by flames.
The moving and the unmoving, beginning with the five seed-syllables,
is the flower; the blossomed lotus is with pollen,
and therein is the semen produced from the union of the couple.
15.15 The methods for consuming that [substance]: free from the hardships of ritual practice (*sādhana*), they bestow accomplishments that would otherwise be difficult to achieve;

and the methods involving flowers and so forth placed upon a lotus, which are free from practices such as incineration (*jvālana*), are for the purpose of identifying the "cattle" (*paśu*) over seven lifetimes.

Due to the union with donkeys and animals, and due to the union with jackals and the like, the offering and consumption [of meat] should be given to the ḍākinīs who bestow the lower and other attainments.
That substance is that semen; "origination" (*saṃbhava*) means consumption.

As for the practice of the fourfold internal [yoga]: by means of the rays from the *hūṃ* syllable situated upon the moon in the *dharmodayā*-lotus below the navel, one agitates the Tathāgatas and others residing in the heart. Then, in this state of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), a sublime and inconceivable worship—free from the distinctions of perceiving form and so forth, inseparable from the five gnoses, and an unstruck oblation (*anāhatāhuti*)—is to be offered as a *bali* to the Ḍākinīs of the seven moments.

In the four wheels of the *yogapīṭha*, because that substance arises there and because the *caru* offering moves through the unstruck (*anāhata*) state by means of the divisions of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, one should offer the external food into the fire of the syllable *HŪṂ* according to the sequence of the external *homa*. Furthermore, one should offer it into the form of non-apprehension (*ānupalambha*). One should offer the external food by means of the sequence of the external *homa*.
"However many," and so forth. One should indeed instruct the disciple in the mantra, mudrā, and so on.
The mantra is the syllable *hūṃ*. 15.20
For that yogin, the procedure for wisdom (prajñā) in the form of midnight is prescribed.

One who is disciplined in the union with the mudrā, consecrated, possessed of knowledge, and observant of the commitments (samayin), being compassionate, should not revile other men who observe the commitments.
The five knowledges, as well as the body with its primary and secondary marks— these are the five bodies. (15.26)

"Having worshipped," and so forth: having fully honored and served the sixteen Yoginīs who are united with the Yogis, and having recited the mantra while endowed with the mudrās, one who is naked, always possessed of wisdom, and seeking that goal, should recite [the mantra] and consume that substance.
"Naked" means devoid of the armor of mantra, mudrā, and so forth; he possesses only the five gnoses.
15.28 The self-messenger (ātmadūtī) and the Sahajasundarī are indeed that very non-duality which is the supreme all; there is nothing else whatsoever.
The self-messenger is the Sahajasundarī;
that substance is the moment of its arising, and its consumption is non-apprehension.

At night, he is manifestly immersed in wisdom (*prajñā*); by day, he is the concealed method (*upāya*), unified. In the state of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), he is manifest as extensive as the expanse of the realm of space; in the maṇḍala circle (*maṇḍalacakra*), he is concealed and conventional.
His own body is clothed in the limbs of living beings; considering that very skin to be his dwelling and home, one who seeks the bliss of the state of Vajradhara should move and meditate upon it.

The rejection and abandonment of the faces of the four [deities], beginning with the white and black Bhagavat, as well as their mantras; "beasts" refers to the sense faculties and their objects; "consuming" refers to the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature.
The perception of the water of the moon;
the setting of the moon—this is the third purity, consisting of all dualities and characterized by non-dual conduct. || 15 ||
Now, "atha" and so forth.
The brother’s practice is the vajra-brother;
from Soma comes non-duality, the consumption of the bindu of the vajra-lotus, and non-dual gnosis.
16.3 Pleasure is semen; pain is passion.
[Sukhaṃ retaḥ] emended by the editor; *sukhacetaḥ* in the manuscript.
"Together" means with; that is to say, they have arisen simultaneously, sharing the same pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, for one who corrupts the mantra or reveals it [to the uninitiated], only the corruption of the mantra itself would have been committed.
The *caru* is prepared in two vessels.
Vāmā is satisfaction and the mind of wisdom;
vāmā means woman;
aṅga means body.
Therefore, one who has embraced the left-handed woman (vāmā) should worship that left-handed woman;
such a practitioner of the left-handed way (vāmācāra), through the worship of women, attains the awakening of the co-emergent (sahaja).
"Vāmamokṣa, Vārāhī, and the seventh moment are nirvāṇa," and so forth.
Without [the need for] recitation, vows, and the like, everything is accomplished through the exhortation of Heruka by means of Vārāhī, who is the nature of the seventh moment. || 16 ||
17. "Atha" and so forth.

Holding the heart-mass and the food-mass at the tip of one’s own nose, one should draw the desired woman in by means of the nasal breath and cause her to enter that mass. Having whirled her around the head by means of the circular movement of the flowing nostrils, and having uttered the *codanā* [impulsion], one should cast her into one’s own throat. *Hṛt piṇḍam*. (ed.)
[The woman] desired by him;
*tatpiṇḍe* [in that mass];
*vahat* [carrying].
[Having recited] *uccārya* (the manuscript reads this; the edition reads *uddhārya*).

Note: The necrophilic practice involves a *pretī*, that is, a corpse (*mṛtakā*) free from wounds and the like. Having bathed her with scented water, one inserts yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and one's own vajra into her womb, and then begins the meditation and recitation (*dhyānajapa*).
Having sprinkled it with scented water, she should perform weeping and so forth.
There, having applied [the substance], she should take the *rocanā* (yellow pigment). By means of that *tilaka*, all are brought under control and attracted.

17.4 *Hetu* and so forth: Having cast yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) into the womb of a girl with tawny eyes, one should meditate upon and recite [the mantra] while united with her until she discharges [the fluid]. By means of a tilaka made from that, people become givers of wealth and other things.
The Blessed One is Varṇābha; the Blessed Lady is Jīvanā. He himself is the bearer of their yoga. At Varṇābha, there is the giving of gifts such as the application of *tilaka* and wealth.
[The manuscript reads *varṇābho*; the edition emends to *varṇābhe*. The manuscript reads *tadyogadhārī*; the edition reads *tat*yogadhārī*.]
Some say that "jīvanā" means the means of reviving the living.

Regarding the passage beginning with "sainyādi": having meditated upon the letter *ra* above the army, one should set it ablaze by means of a circle of wind presided over by the syllable *yaṃ*, which is impelled by the breath from the nose; from that, its destruction occurs. The syllable of emission (*visargākṣara*) is the letter *aḥ*.
The syllable *maḥ* is the weapon (*astra*) and the armor (*kavaca*); the letter *ra* is the supreme weapon (*paramāstra*). || 17 ||
"Then," and so forth.

The "one who knows the procedure" (vidhijña) is the yogin skilled in such rituals for raising the corpse (*śavotthāpana*) or accomplishing the *vetāla*. "Kalpa" means ritual procedure (*vidhi*), practice (*upacāra*); some say it refers to the *tantra*.
One should offer oblations to the heart with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).
Gradually, through the power obtained by means of meditation and recitation, [one attains] the power of raising up corpses in cremation grounds and other such places. || 18 ||
Now, "atha" and so forth.

For the purpose of reciting the mantras of the heart and so forth: "color" refers to caste (jāti), distinguished by [the material of] stone, animal products, or wood; and "number" refers to there being this many beads on the rosary.
"Vajrākṣa" refers to the *vajrākṣa* plant; some say it is a particular kind of tree.
"Bone of Mahīndrapuruṣa" refers to the bone of a person possessing the marks of a great man (*lākṣaṇika*).
The Lord, seated on the lap of the Mahāyoginī, is embraced by the Bhagavatī;
Vajravārāhī, his own consort, is at his left side.
With his power manifested, he shall wander in the Nandana grove together with the yoginīs.
Now, "atha" and so forth. 20.1ff.

One should offer the oblation in non-duality with one’s own mudrā. Milk—that is, cow’s milk—is the substance to be offered; having consecrated it a thousand times at night, one should offer one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) oblations. Now, regarding the phrase "atha" and so forth: having thus consecrated the substance one hundred and eight times, one should present a thousand oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and a hundred oblations with the other mantras. Soma is milk; *bhoga* is the earth. With me, Vārāhī, together with the Blessed One Vīreśvara, there is an offering of great flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*), and not of any other kind of meat. *Padma* is the lotus flower. *Ekaikaṃ* means one by one. 20.
21. Now, beginning with "atha" and so forth...
The hero, the yogin, having brought fire from a caṇḍāla, should kindle it; some say this refers to the fire used for the funeral rites of a caṇḍāla. "In secret" means in a solitary place.

Having raised the *śakti* and drawn the object of the rite (*sādhya*) into the substance to be offered by means of the dispatched *yoginīs*, one should cause them to enter. The reality of the messenger (*dūtī-tattva*) is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) in all phenomena; for one who is fit for that, there is remorse for the sake of destroying evil. In that very context, some say that the destruction of evil occurs through oblations of ghee and other substances, along with recitation (*japa*), performed subsequently. Others say it is pacification (*śānti*). [One should offer] crow feathers soaked in neem juice from the *piśāca-śākhoṭaka* tree—eight hundred plus more than eight hundred.

In the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), the Blessed One is red like vermilion (*sindūra*); the oblation should be smeared with vermilion. At the end of the mantra, the name of that person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) [is inserted] according to one's desire and intention.
The *mudrā* is the desired maiden;
the king of kings is the yogi; he is the embodiment of knowledge and the attainer of power.
By means of these [mudrās] drawn forth,
having performed the sixty-four yogas, he sports with the Mahāmudrā.

This was stated with reference to those of weak and middling faculties. With reference to the practitioner of superior faculty, he says "all," and so forth. One who possesses the *ahaṃkāra* of Heruka; "mudrā" refers to worship that is always non-dual with one's own innate consort (*sahajamudrā*).

Regarding "that very [thing]," and so forth: having slain [the object] with the ray of light from the syllable *HŪṂ*, having led it to the Unstruck (*anāhata*), and having severed all conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) by means of the fire of gnosis (*jñānavahni*), one serves the beautiful woman of non-duality (*advaitasundarī*).
[The variant *sthitvā* in the edition is corrected to *chittvā* based on the manuscript.]
All conceptual constructions are the channels, the innate messengers; there is the yoga of the deity and the yoga of non-duality.
Having struck with fists and so forth.
Having carried [them away], having broken [the armor and so forth], and having cut [them] with his nails and other means; having broken [them],
[and] having cut [them].
Eating and serving. || 21 ||
"Then," and so forth.
Furthermore, a practitioner of the maṇḍala-circle yoga for the accomplishment of a vetāla should offer oblations into the mouth of a corpse;
he should recite the mantra of the specific target with great solemnity.
Or the Blessed One is surrounded by many yoginīs. Then that practitioner moves through the three worlds, and so forth; he is the conqueror of all worlds.
22.9 "Mahā" and so forth: By this sequence, Heruka also attained the state of Vajrasattva.

"Without having recited [the mantra] and without having performed prior service"—this refers to the phrase "entirely," and so forth. Through the meditation on the Space-Vajra, the state of Vajrasattva is accomplished. || 22 ||
23. "Now," and so forth.

A single fragmentary skull is a *kapardaka* (cowrie-shell amulet), or one with a single ear-hole. Having written the body of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) together with their name in the filaments of a hundred-and-fifty-petaled lotus on birch-bark or similar material, and having written the mantra and the name in reverse order on the petals, one should place it within the skull. Likewise, having written another wheel and covered [the first] with it, and having likewise written the mantra on the lotus petals, one should offer each petal individually into the fire while reciting the mantra in reverse order. Having covered it with that, according to the desire of the practitioner, [it is done] in accordance with the intention of the person to be acted upon.

Regarding the passage beginning with *hometyādi*: one should know that when offerings are to be made upon the petals, the Yoginīs have drawn in and caused the target (*sādhya*) to enter. And in the wheel (*cakra*), one should offer the non-dual (*advaya*) oblation (*bali*) with the mudrā. *Ahalyam* means that which must not be done otherwise. One should draw the wheel with one’s own blood and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) upon the heart of an image made of red sandalwood. By "contrary to the rule" (*samayaviparītena*) is meant by a reversed recitation. With golden-colored ochre (*gairika*), the heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī, who possesses all the vidyās, [is written].

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra upon his entire body and engaging in meditative visualization and so forth, the yogin becomes equal to a Tathāgata; [he likewise places] other mantras as well. (23)
Now, "atha" and so forth.

Having bound the Daṃṣṭriṇī mudrā, which is the personal mudrā of Vajravārāhī, and having embraced the yogin whose body is formed by the placement of the seed-syllables and whose physical form consists of the Lord through the placement of mantras—this vidyā is the heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī. By reciting it once together with the name of the target, [one achieves] the summoning of all beings and so forth. One should then cast the written wheel, such as "Expel so-and-so! and so on, from the single wind-maṇḍala yantra into another wind-maṇḍala. || 24 ||
*Tata* and so forth.
The greeting "potaṅgī" is an inquiry after one's arrival; the response "pratipotaṅgī" is a salutation and an expression of a very warm welcome. || 25 ||
26. "Then," and so forth. [This refers to the section beginning with the word *atha*.]
The yogi who knows the ritual procedure understands the means for the realization of the Yoginīs born of the left.
*Cundikā* is a synonym for emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the perfection (*pāramitā*).
The middle finger is the guru of the crest;
the ring finger is the principal;
the little finger is the child.
The tree is the thumb.

In the center are all the heroes and yoginīs; in the middle of the assembly (*melaka*), he who knows the language, the secret signs (*chomma*), and so forth of the leaders of the hosts of heroes, yogins, and yoginīs, is indeed the *ācārya*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the wheel of deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and having made them witnesses, [the teacher] should dismiss [the unqualified] by saying, "This fool is unworthy of this mandala," while wiping the back of the right hand with the left hand. Then, one should feed him elsewhere.

% NB: Expulsion of one unworthy of the *gaṇamaṇḍala*; nevertheless, he is fed elsewhere. "In this way," etc.: one should eat together with the disciples and those who know the pledges (*samaya*) known to oneself. In the midst of the yogins and yoginīs, [one should perform] the dismissal at the back, the palate, and the hands. One should eat the sacrificial pap (*caru*) from the two vessels, which constitutes the manifestation of the *maṇḍala*-circle, together with the disciples and those who know the secret signs (*chommaka*). Likewise for other *maṇḍala*-holders. % NB: There appears to be a hierarchy of disciples here.

In all rites, such as those for pacification and so forth, the previously mentioned mandala-installation is prescribed. The Yoginīs and others are to be stationed according to the sequence of the directions beginning with the south. In due order, for the practitioners devoted to the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*), the Ḍākinīs remain present through their grace.
These are they; he is their [beloved]. By means of the left [hand], the female practitioner (*yoginī*) always reveals her own tradition and the perfected state to the practitioner (*yogin*).
When one has offered salutations and is honored, they attain a state of true being.
With the left hand, she indicates her own direction, that is, her own place of residence.

Regarding the passage beginning with "difficult to obtain" (*durlabha*): through the consumption of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the *ḍākinīs* are seen; they bring about swift accomplishment (*āśusiddhi*). (Note: *aśvasiddhikarāḥ* is corrected to *āśusiddhikarāḥ* by the editor.)
The yogin Vīreśa should observe these mudrās in the house of the Kula;
they are imperishable because there is no exhaustion of the production of love.
They are imperishable because they preserve their own commitment. || 26 ||
*Athetyādi* (Now, etc.). 27.1ff.

The mantra is the heart of the Blessed One. "Sarvavajra" is the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*). That itself is the four-faced one. "Tathā," and so forth. Having performed the protection consisting of the meditation on the mantra and mudrās, such as the armor (*kavaca*), he is adorned and protected. Regarding "upadeśa," and so forth: in the region of the navel, the light-form of the *pramāṇa* wind flows in the form of the *niṣprapañca* bindu, *nāda*, the syllable *oṃ*, the syllable *hūṃ*, and so on.
"By which," and so forth. A single mantra, when recited with such-and-such an intention, bestows all desired fruits accordingly, like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi). || 27 ||
28. "Bestower of all fruits as they are desired," etc.
Now, [the commentary begins with] "atha" and so forth.

Only those who know the reality of well-guarded mantras may undertake supreme yoga. However, practitioners who are engaged in other ritual systems (*kriyātantra*) and so forth are deluded, because [the teachings] conceal the essence of mantras and the like in its entirety for their sake, and because they speak of what is devoid of essence. "Possession by Heruka" (*herukasamāveśa*) is the firm ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) with one's own self as having the form of Heruka through meditative cultivation; [this occurs] by his grace.

*Mudrā* is the convention taught by the Guru; it is both internal and external *prajñā*, as well as the *Prajñāpāramitā*. *Yoga* is practice (*abhyāsa*), and it is also meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). By means of *vāmā*—that is, wisdom (*prajñā*) or a woman—the world, the moving universe, is impelled and produced. *Sevā* (service) is also conduct (*ācāra*), as well as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the knowledge of the three realms of existence.
The *vāma-mantra* is the mantra taught in the *Devītantra*. By the *vāma*, that is, by means of the sequence of the *Vāmātantra*.
(*vāmatantra* is the reading of the edition).

"Yoga," and so forth. The knowledge of yoga is the wisdom of Vajradhara, which is indivisible from emptiness and compassion. For the sake of concealing that [wisdom], the Kriyātantra and other classes were introduced. By means of those respective tantras, practitioners achieve success through afflicted accomplishments (*kliṣṭasiddhi*), but not through Mahāmudrā. "Concealment" refers to that [tantra] in which such concealment occurs; it is for that purpose. The treatise is for the very purpose of introducing them [to the higher path]. For this reason, they neither achieve [supreme success] nor are they liberated. Maturation occurs through the Yoga Tantra; liberation occurs through the Yogottara. (28)
% NB Criticism of *kriyātantras* and their practitioners % NB Hierarchy of tantras: *yogatantra* matures; *yogottara* liberates 29.1ff.
Elsewhere the support was concealed, but here it has been explicitly stated.
